Akari, who had taught Haoran calligraphy for six years, sat across from him with her hands folded. Somewhere between their last lesson and this trip to Kyoto, one of them had promised the other something. Neither could say what. Each suspected the other remembered and was waiting to be reminded. So they watched the rice fields slide past, and the silence between them became a sealed envelope, carried carefully, addressed to both of them, opened by neither. g.passage: Who decides what a nine-year-old is ready to hear? I put that question to Father Thiago on the Clyde bridge in the winter of 1987, though I had not set foot in his church for three years. My younger brother had asked me why our mother no longer came home, and I wanted the priest to give me an answer I could repeat. Thiago leaned on the cold stone and watched the river for a long while. Then he said that a hard truth told gently was a lantern, not a stone; the boy could carry it in front of him instead of on his back. I, Saoirse, the lapsed one, had expected scripture. g.passage: Wind hissed through the pines above the mountain bus stop near Porto Alegre, and my mother, Mingyu, smelled of the orange peel she always chewed when nervous. I was the bride, Booker was the groom, and the only road to the chapel was this one. Every bus would carry me past it. My mother studied the timetable as if it were scripture, then folded it into a small square. Rules are coats, she said at last, cut for the shoulders of whoever first wore them.
